358.title: Jaap for courage
358.hook: many Sikhs turn to Jaap when they need strength
358.howItsDone: Some Sikhs recite or listen to Jaap Sahib when they need strength, before exams, surgery, journeys or hard conversations, as well as in their daily Nitnem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit, and your line, prayer stirred in. Did you say something kind over a meal? Today, what Jaap is for on a hard day. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

The waiting room before the scan. The car outside the job interview. The hallway before the hard conversation with your father. The heart is going too fast, and every bit of advice, just breathe, you've got this, sounds thin. What people actually do in that moment is reach for something. A song with a beat. A friend's voice on the phone. A line they know by heart. Ask some Sikhs what they reach for, and you may hear the same answer. Today: bal.
screen: `THE WAITING ROOM BEFORE THE SCAN.` → `ADVICE SOUNDS THIN.` → `WHAT DO YOU REACH FOR?`

segments.voice: Some Sikhs say that when they need strength, they turn to Jaap Sahib. Before an exam, before surgery, on a long night drive, at a hospital bedside. Some recite it under their breath. Some play a recording in the car. Why Jaap, of all the banis? Three reasons are often given. The first is the words themselves. Jaap is full of the qualities a frightened person needs to hear: ajai, unconquerable; abhai, fearless; alai, indestructible; the protector with weapons in hand; the One who holds even death. Said aloud, those words push back against the weight. The second is the rhythm. You heard it at the drums three days ago. The quick meters make your breath fall into time, and a steadier breath makes the next step easier. The third is the voice. Jaap is the Tenth Guru's. Sikhs know his story: a father executed, a city lost, four sons lost, and Sikh tradition remembers him in chardi kala, rising spirits, through all of it. When a Sikh recites Jaap, they aren't trying to manufacture courage from nothing. They're borrowing it, from a Guru who had every reason to be afraid, and who, as Sikhs remember him, kept going. Notice that Jaap never says the hard thing won't happen. It doesn't promise a good scan or a passed exam. It does something different. Sikhs hear it reminding the one reciting who stands with them while it happens. That's the courage on offer: not certainty about the outcome, but company in it.
screen: `BEFORE THE EXAM, BEFORE THE SURGERY.` · `THE WORDS: UNCONQUERABLE, FEARLESS.` · `THE RHYTHM: BREATH FALLS INTO TIME.` · `THE VOICE: A GURU WHO KEPT GOING.` · then, large: `BORROW THE COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen before something hard. Think of one hard thing coming up, today or this week. If you can, play a minute of Jaap Sahib now, and let the rhythm steady your breath. If you can't, say a few lines you know: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Then picture yourself walking into the hard moment, not alone, with the rhythm still going inside you. Breathe slowly. The bell holds the time.
Bal, strength. Some Sikhs turn to Jaap when they need it, borrowing the Tenth Guru's fearlessness in his own words and rhythm.
Your line: borrow the courage. Today, before one hard thing, take one minute with a line or a song that steadies you, and walk in with it. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

359.title: Why so many names
359.hook: a thousand names say that no single name can hold Him
359.howItsDone: Sikhs call the One by many names in prayer and kirtan, Waheguru, Akal Purakh, Ram, Hari, Gobind, Kartar and more, following the Guru Granth Sahib, which uses names from many languages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bal, and your line, borrow the courage. Did a line or a song walk you into something hard? Today, a step back to look at the whole hymn and ask a simple question. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

How many names do you have? Probably more than you think. Your full name on forms. A shorter one for friends. Something only your grandmother called you. Mom, or Dad, or Auntie, to someone. Babe, to someone else. A nickname from a soccer team that you'd rather forget. Each one is true. Each one holds a different piece of you. And not one of them, on its own, is the whole person. So what happens when the one being named is infinitely larger than any person? Today: asankh naav.
screen: `A NAME ON FORMS, A NAME FOR FRIENDS.` → `WHAT YOUR GRANDMOTHER CALLED YOU.` → `NO ONE NAME IS THE WHOLE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Over the last four weeks you've heard a tiny slice of Jaap's names. Timeless. Merciful. Formless. Unborn. The armed One. Sun of suns. Lamp of beauty. Provider. Gobind. Home of compassion. Fearless. And there are hundreds more you haven't heard yet. Why so many? Jaap answered it in its first stanza: who can tell all Your names? The wise speak the names drawn from Your deeds. So the long list isn't trying to finish the job. It's admitting the job can't be finished, and praising anyway. Each name is a window into one room of a house too big to see all at once. Guru Nanak said the same in Japji. In the nineteenth pauri, he says: countless are Your names, countless Your places. And then he adds that even the word countless is too heavy to carry. Notice too where the names come from. The Guru Granth Sahib calls the One by names from many places: Ram and Hari and Gobind, which Hindus also use; Allah and Khuda and Rahim, which Muslims also use; and the name that became the Sikh word of wonder, Waheguru. Jaap adds Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic names of its own. Sikhs don't treat any one of these as the password. The One, Sikh teaching holds, is beyond them all, and present in each. That's why the carry is more names than stars. Not because anyone has counted. Because, like the stars, the more you look, the more there are.
screen: `HUNDREDS OF NAMES IN ONE HYMN.` · `NO LIST CAN FINISH THE JOB.` · `JAPJI 19: COUNTLESS ARE YOUR NAMES.` · `NAMES FROM MANY LANGUAGES.` · then, large: `MORE NAMES THAN STARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write three names for the Divine. Grab a pen or open a note. Write three names. They can be ones you've learned here, like Akal or Kripaal, ones from your own background, or deed-names from your own life, like the one who carried me last winter. If the word Divine doesn't fit you, write three names for whatever you feel grateful toward. Read them slowly. Notice that each one opens a different window. Then sit with all three. The bell holds the time.
Asankh naav, countless names. Because no single name can hold the One: Jaap's hundreds of names admit the list can never be finished, and praise anyway.
Your line: more names than stars. Tonight, if you can see the sky, look up and count a few stars, and let each one stand for one more name. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

360.title: The whole Jaap
360.hook: all 199 stanzas take about fifteen to twenty minutes
360.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the whole of Jaap Sahib every morning, from memory or a gutka, in about fifteen to twenty minutes, and many others listen to recordings while traveling or getting ready for the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asankh naav, and your line, more names than stars. Did you write three of your own? Today, all of them at once: the whole hymn, start to finish. Day three hundred sixty.

You've seen a cathedral, or a gurdwara, or a mountain, in pieces. A photo of a doorway. A close-up of a carving. One window, one dome. Then one day you stand across the street, or on the far side of the valley, and see the whole thing at once, and every piece suddenly makes sense where it sits. For four weeks you've looked at Jaap Sahib one window at a time. A word here, a meter there. Today you step back across the valley. Today: naam.
screen: `A BUILDING SEEN IN PIECES.` → `THEN, ACROSS THE VALLEY, ALL OF IT.` → `EVERY PIECE MAKES SENSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the map. Recited at a steady pace, all one hundred ninety-nine stanzas take about fifteen to twenty minutes. It opens with one big stanza, the chhappai, that clears the table: no mark, no caste, no lineage; king of kings; named by deeds. Then the snake begins to glide. Bhujang prayat: namastvam akaale, namastvam kripaale, salutation after salutation. Then the meter shortens to the quick two-word steps of chachari: aroop hain, anoop hain, ajoo hain, abhoo hain. Further along, the language turns to Persian and Arabic, and you meet the lamp of beauty and the giver of daily bread. Longer rolling lines, roaal, bring one form, many sights. The tiny harbolmana lines give the home of compassion and the breaker of the cruel. The one-letter meter flies: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Between them, other meters you haven't met yet, each with its own walk. And the end returns to the glide, gathering everything into sadaa sachidaanand, and the last words, ever by your side. Seen whole, the shape is clear. It begins by saying what the One isn't, then spends nearly two hundred stanzas saying what the One does and is, in rhythm after rhythm and in more than one language, and ends by saying the One is right here. That's why many Sikhs say Jaap is best understood not by studying it in pieces, but by saying it whole, every morning, until it lives in the body. The pieces you've learned, akaal, kripaal, aroop, abhai, are signposts along that road.
screen: `FIFTEEN TO TWENTY MINUTES, 199 STANZAS.` · `CHHAPPAI, GLIDE, QUICK STEPS, PERSIAN.` · `TINY LINES, ONE LETTER, THE GLIDE AGAIN.` · `WHAT HE ISN'T, WHAT HE IS, HE'S HERE.` · then, large: `ALL THE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to it whole. The bell will give you two minutes now; the whole Jaap needs about fifteen to twenty. So start it now, if you can, and let it play past the bell, or set aside a quiet stretch later today. As you listen, don't translate. Just notice the meters change, like a road changing from gravel to pavement to dirt. When you hear a word you know, akaal, kripaal, abhai, smile at it as it passes. The bell holds the time.
Naam, name. One hundred ninety-nine stanzas, about fifteen to twenty minutes: from no mark and no caste, through every meter and language, to ever by your side.
Your line: all the names. Today, find fifteen or twenty minutes, on a walk, a commute, a quiet evening, and let the whole hymn play through once. Day three hundred sixty.

361.title: Jaap close
361.hook: the Tenth Guru's praise now sits beside Nanak's Japji in your morning
361.howItsDone: In the Sikh morning Nitnem, Japji Sahib is recited first and Jaap Sahib second, followed by the Tav Prasad Savaiye; many Sikhs say all three before or around dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam, and your line, all the names. Did the whole hymn play through once? Today, the last day of our thirty with Jaap Sahib. Day three hundred sixty-one.

Some mornings have a shape you could recognize in the dark. Feet on the cold floor. Water on the face. The kettle. The same mug. In Sikh homes that keep Nitnem, the shape has words too, and they come in a fixed order. First a quiet, thoughtful voice, the first Guru's. Then a faster one, written generations later, with a drumbeat in it. One after the other, every morning, for generations. Thirty days ago you only knew the first. Today: nitnem.
screen: `A MORNING YOU'D KNOW IN THE DARK.` → `FIRST A QUIET VOICE.` → `THEN A FASTER ONE WITH A DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: Put the two side by side. Japji is Guru Nanak's, the first Guru. It opens the Guru Granth Sahib, on page one. Jaap is Guru Gobind Singh's, the tenth Guru. It opens the Dasam Granth. Two first pages, two Gurus many generations apart. Japji begins with Ik Onkar, One, and the Mool Mantar: true Name, creator, without fear, without hatred, timeless, unborn. Jaap begins with no mark, no caste, and then salutes the One as akaal, abhai, ajooni. Same truths, different walk. Japji thinks its way forward, pauri by pauri, asking questions. Jaap marches, name after name, through many meters and languages. Sikhs believe the same light, the same jot, passed from Guru Nanak to each Guru in turn. Saying Japji and then Jaap each morning is a small way of hearing that: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth, and the light in both. Now look back at the road. The morning praise, Jaap Sahib. No mark, no caste. King of kings. Named by deeds. The snake's gait. Akaal, the Timeless. The Merciful. Formless, beyond compare. Ajooni, unborn. The armed One, the protector. Sun of suns. Song of songs. The lamp of beauty. The provider. Gobind. One form, many sights. Ender and sustainer. Karunaa, the house of compassion. Breaker of the cruel. The one-letter meter. Abhai. Every land. Beyond the fear of death. Keeping the pace. The last stanza. The amrit bowl. Courage. So many names. The whole Jaap. Tomorrow, the third morning bani, ten verses under the heading by your grace.
screen: `JAPJI OPENS ONE GRANTH, JAAP THE OTHER.` · `THE FIRST GURU, THEN THE TENTH.` · `ONE LIGHT, ONE JOT, IN BOTH.` · `THIRTY DAYS OF NAMES.` · then, large: `JAPJI, THEN JAAP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add Jaap to your mornings, in whatever size fits. Sit and picture tomorrow morning: where you'll be, what you'll do first. Now picture the place where a few lines of Jaap could go. Maybe a recording while you dress. Maybe the four words, ajai, alai, abhai, abai, at the window. Maybe the full fifteen minutes, if your life allows. Choose one, and promise it gently, for tomorrow only. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Nitnem, the daily rule of prayer. Thirty days with the Tenth Guru's morning praise, which now sits beside Guru Nanak's Japji: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth.
Your line: japji, then jaap. Tomorrow morning, give a minute to each, in that order, even if it's just one line of each. Day three hundred sixty-one. Jaap, done.

362.title: By your grace
362.hook: the heading means by Your grace; ten verses follow
362.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning after Jaap Sahib, and they are among the five banis read while amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jaap closed: the Tenth Guru's praise, nitnem, took its seat beside Nanak's Japji, and your line was japji, then jaap. Did a few of those many names come back to you this morning? Today a new bani begins. Day three hundred sixty-two.

Stand in line at a gurdwara near the end of the service and watch people's hands. A sevadar comes down the row with a bowl of warm karah prasad, the sweet made of flour, ghee and sugar. Nobody reaches in and takes a scoop. Each person holds out two cupped hands, and a spoonful is placed in them. Even a toddler learns the gesture: hands together, open, waiting. You don't earn it at the counter. You receive it. Keep that picture of open hands, because the next bani of the Sikh morning has that same word written over its door. Today: cupped hands, waiting.
screen: `A BOWL OF WARM KARAH PRASAD.` → `TWO HANDS, CUPPED AND OPEN.` → `RECEIVED, NOT TAKEN.`

segments.voice: Tav prasad. Tav means your, and prasad means grace, favor, a gift freely given. It's the same prasad as the sweet in your hands at the gurdwara, and the same word that closes the Mool Mantar at the top of the Japji: gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. Guru Gobind Singh writes tav prasad as a heading again and again in his compositions, over section after section, the way someone might write a dedication at the top of every page. Here it heads ten short poems, the Tav Prasad Savaiye. A savaiya is a verse form, four long, swinging lines, made for reciting aloud. These ten come from the Tenth Guru's Akal Ustat, the praise of the Timeless One, and they're written in Braj, a literary language of north India in his day. Sikhs who keep Nitnem say them every morning, right after the Jaap. They're also among the five banis recited while the amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation. Here's what's surprising. You'd expect a heading like by your grace to be followed by soft, comforting verses. Instead the ten savaiye march past everything people in the Guru's world admired: ascetics and yogis, elephants hung with gold, emperors with beating drums, pilgrims at every river, rituals of every kind. And after each parade, the verses set it all down and say, in effect, that without the Lord's love and grace it weighs nothing. So the heading is the key. Everything that follows is a list of what people try to achieve. The heading names what can only be received. Over the next week we'll take the parade one float at a time.
screen: `TAV PRASAD: BY YOUR GRACE.` · `THE SAME PRASAD AS THE SWEET.` · `TEN SAVAIYE, AFTER THE JAAP.` · `A PARADE OF WHAT PEOPLE ADMIRE.` · then, large: `BY YOUR GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open your hands. Sit comfortably and rest your hands in your lap, palms up, cupped a little, the way people hold them for karah prasad. Breathe slowly. Now notice three things you're holding right now that you didn't make yourself. The breath going in. The light in the room. The fact that you woke up today. Let each one land in your open hands. If you pray, you can whisper Waheguru as you notice each one. And later today, if you can, find a recording of all ten savaiye and listen through, start to finish. The bell holds the time.
Tav prasad. By your grace: the heading the Tenth Guru writes over these ten verses, from the same prasad as the gurdwara's sweet and the Japji's gur prasad.

Your line: cupped hands, waiting. Today, when something good comes to you that you didn't plan or earn, a kind word, a green light, a good meal, say those three words under your breath. Day three hundred sixty-two.

363.title: The ascetics I have seen
363.hook: the poet has seen hosts of monks, siddhas and yogis, yet without love for the Lord it is all worth nothing (Savaiye 1)
363.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya each morning as the first of the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye, and it is often explained in the gurdwara as a warning against outward religion without love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tav prasad, and your line, cupped hands, waiting. Did something good arrive today that you didn't plan for? Now the first of the ten verses. Day three hundred sixty-three.

A traveler has made it his business to see every holy person in the land. He's sat outside the huts of ascetics who've given up everything. He's watched yogis hold impossible postures for hours. He's met celibates, wonder-workers, wandering monks, holy men of every order, in every region he could reach. Some of them were truly impressive. Some of them could do things you and I can't. At the end of all that traveling, he sits down to write what he's learned, and it comes out in one breath. Today: prem.
screen: `A TRAVELER WHO HAS SEEN THEM ALL.` → `ASCETICS, YOGIS, MONKS.` → `WHAT DID HE LEARN?`

segments.voice: That traveler is the voice of the first savaiya. In paraphrase, it goes like this: I have wandered and seen hosts of pure ascetics, siddhas, the dwellings of yogis and celibates. I have seen heroes and gods and sages, and the holy men of sect after sect, the religious ways of every country. Then the last line turns, and it's the whole point: without the love and grace of the Lord, all of this isn't worth one ratti. A ratti is a tiny red seed, used as a small weight for gold. So the verse puts the whole parade of holiness on a jeweler's scale, and without love the pan doesn't tip. Now, this is easy to hear wrong. It isn't sneering at discipline. The poet went out to see these people. Sikh teaching favors the householder's life over the cave, but this verse doesn't sneer at those who chose the cave. The savaiya's point is narrower and harder. A person can sit for years, give up food, give up sleep, and if love isn't at the center of it, the verse says it's weightless. And notice, the savaiya isn't only about other people's practices. Sikhs often hear it as a mirror too: early rising, long recitations, a person's own discipline can go on the same scale. Said in the morning, before the day's practice begins, the verse asks what's at the center of it. The answer it gives is one word. Love.
screen: `HE HAS SEEN EVERY KIND OF HOLY ONE.` · `WITHOUT LOVE, NOT ONE RATTI.` · `NOT A SNEER AT DISCIPLINE.` · `A MIRROR FOR THE MORNING.` · then, large: `NOTHING WITHOUT LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing with love, not show. Settle in and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you'll do today that could be done either way. Making someone's coffee. Answering a hard message. Helping at home. Picture doing it the show way: wanting it noticed, keeping a little count. Then picture doing it the other way, for the person, with nothing in it for you. Notice how different the two feel, even in your imagination. If you pray, you can let Waheguru rest on your breath. Then choose the second way, and when the moment comes today, do it like that. The bell holds the time.
Prem, love. The first savaiya: a traveler sees every kind of holy discipline, and weighs it all without love at less than one ratti, a jeweler's tiny seed.

Your line: nothing without love. Today, before one thing you do for someone, check what's at the center of it. If it's love, carry on. If it's show, start again quietly. Day three hundred sixty-three.

364.title: Elephants in gold
364.hook: drunken elephants decked in gold, horses swift as deer, kings in glory, and all leave this world empty-handed (Savaiye 2)
364.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this as the second of the ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning; it is often explained as a reminder that wealth and power stay behind when a person dies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prem, and your line, nothing without love. This week you closed the Jaap: courage borrowed, more names than stars, all the names, japji then jaap. Then the savaiye opened: cupped hands, waiting, and nothing without love. Today, the second verse. Day three hundred sixty-four.

The parade comes down the road and the crowd goes quiet. First the elephants, huge and swaying, drunk on their own strength, hung with gold so that they flash in the sun. Then the horses, thousands of them, quick as deer, barely touching the ground. Then the kings, broad in the shoulder, and on either side of them, rows and rows of people bowing their heads. Nobody in the crowd can look away. And then the poet leans over and whispers one question. Today: maate matang.
screen: `ELEPHANTS FLASHING WITH GOLD.` → `HORSES QUICK AS DEER.` → `KINGS, AND ROWS OF BOWED HEADS.`

segments.voice: That's the second savaiya. In paraphrase: maddened elephants decked in gold, tall and matchless. Horses by the million, leaping like deer, outrunning the wind. Mighty kings before whom countless heads bow. Then the question: and what of it? Such great kings there have been, and at the end they went away barefoot. Barefoot. That's the picture the verse uses. In the Guru's world, a king never walked anywhere. He rode. So the one who arrived on an elephant leaves on his own bare feet, carrying nothing. Empty-handed, the way everyone leaves. Here's what keeps this from being easy moralizing. Guru Gobind Singh knew this world from the inside. He held court at Anandpur. He rode fine horses, and Sikh tradition tells of an elephant called Prasadi, brought to the young Guru as a gift. He wasn't a poor man shaking his fist at the palace. He was someone who'd seen the gold up close and knew what it could and couldn't do. Notice too what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say elephants are evil, or that horses are sinful, or that owning beautiful things is wrong. Sikhs aren't asked to give up their homes or their work. The savaiya simply follows the parade to its end, past the gates of the city, to the last walk every king takes. And on that walk the gold stays behind. The verse doesn't say here what should be carried instead. It leaves the question standing at the city gate: if not the gold, then what?
screen: `ELEPHANTS, HORSES, BOWING HEADS.` · `AT THE END, THEY LEFT BAREFOOT.` · `THE GURU KNEW THE GOLD UP CLOSE.` · `NOT A BAN ON BEAUTIFUL THINGS.` · then, large: `THEY LEFT EMPTY-HANDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one thing you own and smile. Pick it up if you can: a watch, a mug, your phone, a ring. Hold it and really look at it. Where it came from, what it's been through with you. Breathe slowly. Now let yourself enjoy it, honestly, without guilt. Then let a second thought sit beside the first: one day it won't be yours. Not as a sad thought. As a light one. Smile at it the way you'd smile at a friend you know you'll part from one day. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you set it down. The bell holds the time.
Maate matang, maddened elephants. The second savaiya's parade of power: elephants, horses and bowing heads, and kings who still left this world barefoot.
Your line: they left empty-handed. Today, when you catch yourself wanting something shiny, picture the barefoot king, and see if the wanting gets a little lighter. Day three hundred sixty-four.
